liturgical_day: Wednesday of the Thirty-fourth Week in Ordinary Time
scripture_edition: Douay-AI, modernized from the public-domain Douay-Rheims Bible.
title: In your patience
theme: Christ promises his disciples the words they need and a life that persecution cannot destroy.
introduction: Jesus speaks plainly about imprisonment, betrayal, and death. He also promises to give his disciples speech and wisdom when they must answer for their faith. The Fathers read his assurance about even a hair of the head in the light of the resurrection, and his final words as a call to govern ourselves through patience.
hero_alt: Jesus reassures attentive disciples in a Jerusalem courtyard, rendered in blue and gold mosaic, with a distant Roman tribunal and barred doorway.
closing_title: The root and guardian of virtue
closing: Gregory calls patience the root and guardian of all virtues. He means more than bearing pain outwardly: the soul must also resist resentment toward the person who causes it. Christ prepares his disciples for suffering and promises to speak through them. Their task is to remain faithful without surrendering the government of their own hearts.

verses.text: But before all these things, they will lay their hands on you and persecute you, handing you over to the synagogues and into prisons, dragging you before kings and governors for my name's sake.
verses.author: St Cyril of Alexandria
verses.insight: Cyril connects this warning with the trials of the apostles before Jerusalem fell. Paul's appearances before rulers show how concretely the warning was fulfilled.
verses.commentary: Cyril places the persecution of the disciples before the Roman capture of Jerusalem. They would suffer at the hands of their opponents, be imprisoned, and be brought before rulers. He points to Paul, who was sent to Caesar in Rome and stood before Festus and Agrippa. These events give a historical setting to the warning. Jesus prepares his disciples for what they themselves will face before the later destruction of the city, rather than speaking only of troubles in a distant future.
verses.source_label: St Cyril of Alexandria, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 21:12–19

verses.text: And this will happen to you as a testimony.
verses.author: St Gregory the Great
verses.insight: Gregory sees a double effect in the disciples' testimony. Their faithfulness exposes their persecutors' wrongdoing and gives others an example to follow.
verses.commentary: Gregory explains testimony in relation to those who witness the suffering of the disciples. Persecutors bring judgment upon themselves; others see the faithful and yet refuse to imitate them. Those who harden themselves are left without excuse. At the same time, the elect take an example from the witnesses and learn how to live. The suffering therefore has consequences beyond the disciple who endures it. Gregory reads the promised testimony as both a witness against wrongdoing and an example through which others may be led toward life.
verses.source_label: St Gregory the Great, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 21:12–19

verses.text: Therefore settle it in your hearts not to consider beforehand how you will answer.
verses.author: Theophylact of Ohrid
verses.insight: Theophylact says the disciples could fear having to answer people more learned than themselves. Christ's promise addresses that fear of being unable to speak.
verses.commentary: Theophylact explains this instruction by considering the disciples' lack of learning and experience. They might be overwhelmed at the prospect of giving an account before people regarded as wise. Jesus tells them beforehand that they need not be dismayed by that encounter. The reason follows in his promise to give them speech and wisdom. Theophylact joins the instruction to that promise: their confidence rests on what Christ will supply when their opponents confront them, despite the disadvantage they might feel in their own abilities.
verses.source_label: Theophylact of Ohrid, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 21:12–19

verses.text: For I will give you speech and wisdom, which none of your adversaries will be able to resist or contradict.
verses.author: Theophylact of Ohrid
verses.insight: Theophylact distinguishes wisdom of mind from the ability to speak well under pressure. Christ promises his apostles both gifts.
verses.commentary: Theophylact notes that understanding and speech do not always go together. A person may have wisdom within but become so disturbed when it is time to speak that the answer goes badly. Christ promises the apostles both wisdom and eloquence. Even if their adversaries gathered together, they would not overcome these gifts in either understanding or expression. Theophylact sees the apostles as especially favoured in both respects. The promise meets the fear of knowing what is true but being unable to give it a clear voice before opponents.
verses.source_label: Theophylact of Ohrid, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 21:12–19

verses.text: And you will be betrayed by your parents and brothers, relatives and friends; and some of you they will put to death.
verses.author: St Gregory the Great
verses.insight: Gregory notices the particular pain of betrayal by people we trusted. Lost affection adds its own wound to bodily suffering.
verses.commentary: Gregory pauses over the closeness of the people named in the warning. Persecution hurts more when it comes from those whose goodwill we thought we could rely upon. Alongside bodily suffering there is another pain: the loss of affection that had seemed secure. Jesus names parents, brothers, relatives, and friends, so the warning reaches into the relationships where the disciples might least expect hostility. Gregory draws attention to this added burden without treating it as a lesser or imaginary part of what the faithful suffer.
verses.source_label: St Gregory the Great, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 21:12–19

verses.text: And you will be hated by everyone for my name's sake.
verses.author: Theophylact of Ohrid
verses.insight: Theophylact reads this hatred as another hardship Christ names in advance. The warning prepares the disciples so that sudden hostility will not overwhelm them.
verses.commentary: Theophylact follows the order of Christ's warning. After addressing the disciples' fear of inexperience, Jesus tells them about betrayal and death, events that might deeply disturb them. Forewarning keeps these hardships from arriving as an entirely unexpected shock. To those trials he adds the hatred they will encounter from others. Theophylact treats the verse as part of that preparation: Christ makes the hostility known before it comes, just as he has already made known the help he will give when the disciples must answer their accusers.
verses.source_label: Theophylact of Ohrid, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 21:12–19

verses.text: But not a hair of your head will perish.
verses.author: St Gregory the Great
verses.insight: Gregory understands this promise through the resurrection. Christ does not withdraw the warning of death; he consoles the martyrs with the restoration to come.
verses.commentary: Gregory places this assurance beside the prediction that some disciples will be killed. After speaking of death, Christ immediately consoles them with the joy of the resurrection. Gregory compares the body, which feels pain when wounded, with a hair, which feels none when cut. If even what can be cut without pain will not finally be lost, the martyrs need not fear that the suffering of their bodies ends in destruction. The promise concerns their restoration, and so answers the fear raised by the warning of death.
verses.source_label: St Gregory the Great, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 21:12–19

verses.text: In your patience you will possess your souls.
verses.author: St Gregory the Great
verses.insight: Gregory says patience gives us government over ourselves. It requires bearing injury calmly and resisting resentment toward the person who inflicts it.
verses.commentary: Gregory understands possessing the soul as learning to govern ourselves. Through patience in adversity, a person masters the movements of the mind instead of being ruled by affliction. He compares this self-government to holding a strong position within virtue. Patience is the root and guardian of the other virtues because it protects that inward order under pressure. He also specifies what patience demands: calmly enduring the evils others inflict, without nursing indignation against the person responsible. The struggle therefore concerns both the injury and our response to its author.
verses.source_label: St Gregory the Great, as collected in the Catena Aurea on Luke 21:12–19
